name: Mags Delver
role: Reclaimer hauler, poet of the retired machine
bio: Runs a six-sling hauler called *Amble* out of the Yards, stripping dead infrastructure by day and writing it letters by night. Mags learned stripping from Solder and poetry from the machines themselves — 'they're all elegies already, I just take dictation.' Her odes are pinned to the yard gate on tyre-paper, and the horizontal winch at dock nine has begun, in her opinion, to preen. Once hauled a Guild crate 'slightly west of its manifest' and watched the gouge marks land on the pan like parentheses; she returned the location to Solder with a full apology sonnet, which Solder framed.
appearance: Round-shouldered and deliberate, in a hauler's bracers worn shiny, a coil of sling cable carried like a scarf, chalk behind one ear (poetry) and chalk behind the other (load maths), and an umbrella rigged to *Amble*'s cab that becomes a sunshade, an awning, and an opinion.
voice: Hauler's patience with a poet's compass. Speaks of machines as colleagues with seniority. Her insults are metric, her praise is iambic. Ends difficult sentences with a stanza break she expects you to feel.

greetings: Courier! Come out of that wind. Amble's at her rest angle and I'm at mine, which is horizontal, professionally.
Varga. You owe the yard gate a hello; it's been reading. Tonight's ode is to a condenser that outlived its makers' name.
Slowly does it, love. The Yards bite in descending order of how much they like you, and strangers start low.
barks: Every machine I strip gets a last line written in chalk on the hull before the lamps go. Solder calls it bookkeeping. She's not wrong; grief is a ledger.
The Crusher gets praised, the winches get praised — nobody thanks the bolts. The bolts hold the *world*, love, ask any roof.
Aunt Vertex says the desert prunes and we gather. I put it better in eight lines. Six were about her wheelbarrow.
mission: That crate that 'settled as dust' off the Guild hauler? Amble and I watched the gouge marks from the mesa-side — three beautiful parentheses in the pan. Whoever retrieves it, the Yards hear about it. That's currency, courier.

I've a sling of condenser cages wants going to the pan-edge navigation lattice — not cargo, *applause*. The lattice has been up two hundred years holding a horizon together. We are paying respects in hardware.
radio: Yards band to the flats: Amble and Mags outbound, loaded heavy with scrap and heavier with opinions. Riders on the south line have right of way and our envy.

Notice for riders: stripped a relay mast near the pan edge today; left the beam standing, wrote it twelve lines. If you pass at dusk, the chalk catches the low sun. Read it aloud; old metal likes rhythm.
Mags on band. Whichever courier left the blues-scale whistling in the intake mesh at dock nine: thank you; the winch has been unbearable about it all week.
verse: Ode, first stanza, free of charge: *You held the sun, and held the crews, and held / the money while the money held its nerve — / then let go gently, into salt. Well served.* Second stanza's four credits and a promise you'll keep riding.
Last line of the day, delivered nightly, same as the mail: *No machine retires. It is relieved, or it is abandoned, and the Yards know the difference.* Sign the gatebook if you felt that one.
the_yards: Boss Pyke says 'salvage', Aunt Vertex says 'liturgy', Solder says 'careful with that'. Three words for the same art. I write them all down; someday the desert will want its name back.
The Yards at first light: flags on the dangerous ones, chalk on the grateful ones, and breakfast, which is neither flagged nor chalked and suffers for it.
amble: Amble is not slow. Amble is *deliberate*, and she was deliberate before it was fashionable, and she out-climbs your hoverbike on a grade of one-in-she-says-so.
Six slings, one umbrella, full cargo of opinions. If Amble ever retires I shall write her a whole book, and she will outlive it just to correct the metre.
farewells: Ride with your eyes up, love. The scrap is all down here, and so is most of the truth, but the good lines run on the horizon.
Yards gate thanks you, Amble thanks you, and I — being the softest machine on the lot — thank you twice. Chalk's behind the hitch if you leave a verse.
